chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: rectangles first, then triangles as half rectangles, then every other shape cut into rectangles and triangles. Each formula is earned by a cut and a rearrange before it is used, and each is checked on a figure the student can count.

points.text: Each idea opens with a guess: which rectangle needs more powder, which triangle is bigger, will the area change when the shape slides. The video or the interactive step then checks the guess.
points.title: Predict, then check

points.text: Dissection is the engine of the chapter. A parallelogram, a rhombus and a trapezium are each cut and moved into a rectangle or parallelogram of the same area before any formula is written.
points.title: Cut and rearrange

points.text: Every formula uses a height that meets the base at a right angle, never a slanting side. Obtuse triangles and slanting trapeziums are handled by subtracting or adding pieces.
points.title: Height is perpendicular

points.text: Four interactive tools, each used once: stretching rectangles, sliding a triangle's top vertex, cutting a parallelogram and joining two trapeziums. Other topics are taught by worked examples.
points.title: Tools only where the moving is the idea

modules.module_summary: Area counts unit squares, so a rectangle is length times width and perimeter cannot stand in for area. A triangle is half of a rectangle on the same base and height, and that one formula finds altitudes, splits shapes into equal parts and explains triangles between parallel lines.

content.text:
7.1 Rectangle and Squares
How many different ways can you divide a square into 4 parts of equal area?
One can actually think of infinitely many such ways! Consider a division, such as, and alter each part as follows.
In each part, the area is compressed along one edge and expanded along another edge. If both the compression and expansion are of the same magnitude, then all 4 parts still have the same area!
Try to think of different creative ways to divide a square into 4 parts of equal area.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many ways can a square be cut into 4 parts of equal area? Two? Five? More?
2. Four small squares is one way. Push a notch into one edge of each part and push the same bump out of another edge: the shapes change, the areas do not.
3. Since every notch can be a different shape, there are infinitely many ways. Equal area does not mean equal shape. So what exactly is area, and how do we measure it?

media.instructions_for_student: Area counts unit squares inside a shape, perimeter measures its boundary. Two rectangles can share a perimeter and have different areas, and a rectangle with a longer boundary can still cover fewer squares.
media.description:
A square grid fills the screen with a blue rectangle sitting on its bottom left corner. Its right edge and top edge carry drag handles that snap to grid lines. Four separate readouts show the length, the width, the area and the perimeter, and each one updates the moment the student drags. Beside the blue rectangle sits a pale ghost rectangle, the one to beat, with its own four readouts, so two rectangles can always be compared side by side.

Every card starts with a prediction. In the first card the ghost is 7 by 4 and the student's rectangle is 8 by 3, and the student says which one needs more rangoli powder before any square is counted. Pressing Check shades the unit squares in both and counts them, 28 and 24. A wrong guess shows both counts side by side. The student then drags the edges and sees that the area and the perimeter change by different amounts, and sometimes in different directions.

A Hold perimeter switch locks the perimeter at 20. With it on, pulling one edge longer pushes the other shorter, and the student stretches the rectangle from 5 by 5, which covers 25 squares, down to a thin 9 by 1 strip that covers only 9. As the strip gets thinner the area readout turns red, so the student watches the area fall while the boundary stays the same length. The second and third cards ask for the largest and the smallest area at perimeter 20. The fourth card sets the ghost at 5 by 4, perimeter 18 and area 20, and asks for a rectangle with a larger perimeter but a smaller area. A 10 by 1 strip does it, with perimeter 22 and area 10, and when the student finds such a pair the tool marks it as a longer boundary with less area. In the fifth card the area is 21 and one side is 7, and the student drags the other side until the area reads 21; the tool checks by multiplying back, 7 times 3. In the sixth card the tool draws the diagonal of a 7 by 4 rectangle and the student counts the squares in one triangle, 14, which is half of 28.

Hints go in order. First: what does area count, and what does perimeter measure? Then: count the unit squares inside, then walk around the edge and add the sides. Then: for a 10 by 1 strip the perimeter is 22 but the area is only 10, so compare it with 5 by 4. Last, the pair is shown with both counts and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that area and perimeter measure different things, that one can grow while the other shrinks, and that the length of the boundary can never stand in for the number of squares inside.

You might have seen the rangoli art form, in which regions of different shapes are beautifully coloured using rangoli powder.
Which of these rectangles requires more rangoli powder to be coloured, if the colouring is done evenly?
Clearly, the rectangle having sidelengths 7 cm and 4 cm contains 7 × 4 = 28 unit squares, and the rectangle having sidelengths 8 cm and 3 cm contains 8 × 3 = 24 unit squares.
Area of a rectangle = length × width.
The areas of the rectangles as seen in the previous problem are generally written as 28 sq. cm and 24 sq. cm, or as 28 cm² and 24 cm².

content.text:
What is the area of each triangle in this rectangle?
We have seen that the diagonal of a rectangle divides it into two congruent triangles. So, the area of each triangle is half the area of the rectangle.
In terms of unit squares, half the area fills exactly half the number of unit squares.
So the area of each triangle is 1/2 × 7 × 4 = 14 cm².

content.text:
Why do we count the number of unit squares to assign measures for area? Couldn't we have just used the perimeter of a region, i.e., the length of its boundary as a measure of its area?
If two regions have the same perimeter, can't we conclude that they have the same area? Or, if one region has a larger perimeter than another region, can't we conclude that it also has a larger area?
The perimeter of a region is not indicative of its area. The reason is that regions can have the same perimeter but different areas, and vice versa.
Perimeter of Region 1 > Perimeter of Region 2, but Area of Region 1 < Area of Region 2.
Find two rectangles that are examples of such regions. If needed, use a grid paper for this.

content.text:
Worked example: Compare a 10 cm by 1 cm strip with a 5 cm by 4 cm rectangle: perimeter and area.
1. Strip perimeter: 2 × (10 + 1) = 22 cm. Strip area: 10 × 1 = 10 cm².
2. Rectangle perimeter: 2 × (5 + 4) = 18 cm. Rectangle area: 5 × 4 = 20 cm².
3. 22 > 18 but 10 < 20.
Answer: The strip has the larger perimeter (22 cm) but the smaller area (10 cm²)

content.text:
Worked example: Compare a 4 by 4 square with a thin zigzag made of 9 unit squares joined edge to edge in one line with bends.
1. Square: perimeter 4 × 4 = 16 units, area 16 square units.
2. Zigzag: each square shares edges with its neighbours, leaving 2 × 9 + 2 = 20 unit edges on the boundary, so perimeter 20 units.
3. Zigzag area: 9 square units.
Answer: The zigzag has the larger perimeter (20 units against 16) but the smaller area (9 against 16)

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 2): A path (the shaded portion) is laid around a rectangular park EFGH inside a rectangle ABCD. (i) What measurements do you need to find the area of the path? Assign values and give a formula. (ii) If the width of the path along each side is given, can you find its area? If not, what else do you need? (iii) Does the area of the path change when the outer rectangle is moved while keeping the park inside it?
1. (i) Measure the length and width of ABCD and of EFGH.
2. Area of path = area of ABCD − area of EFGH. With ABCD 20 m by 14 m and EFGH 16 m by 10 m: 20 × 14 − 16 × 10 = 280 − 160 = 120 m².
3. (ii) The widths alone are not enough; we also need the park's length and width. With a park 16 m by 10 m and widths 2 m on every side, break the path into two long strips 20 m by 2 m and two short strips 10 m by 2 m: 2 × 40 + 2 × 20 = 120 m².
4. (iii) Moving ABCD around the park changes the widths but not the two rectangles, so the path area stays the same.
Answer: (i) Path area = area of ABCD − area of EFGH (120 m² for the chosen values). (ii) Also need the park's sides; same 120 m². (iii) No, the area does not change

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 3): A plot has sides 14 m and 12 m with a crosspath. What other measurements do you need to find the area of the crosspath? Assign values and give a formula.
1. We need the widths of the two paths: p for the path along the 14 m side and q for the path along the 12 m side.
2. The two strips are 14 × p and 12 × q, but they overlap in a p by q square counted twice.
3. Area = 14p + 12q − pq. With p = 1 m and q = 2 m: 14 × 1 + 12 × 2 − 1 × 2 = 14 + 24 − 2 = 36 m².
Answer: The widths of the two paths; area = 14p + 12q − pq, which is 36 m² when the widths are 1 m and 2 m

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 4): Find the area of the spiral tube shown in the figure. The tube has the same width (1 unit) throughout, and its straight parts measure 20, 20, 20, 15, 15, 10, 10, 5 and 5 along the outside.
1. The hint: an L shaped tube with arms 5 and 5 has the same area as a straight tube of length 5 + 5 − 1 = 9, because the corner square is counted in both arms.
2. Add all the straight lengths: 20 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 120.
3. There are 8 bends, each counted twice, so subtract 8: 120 − 8 = 112.
4. The straightened tube is 112 units long and 1 unit wide: 112 × 1 = 112.
Answer: 112 square units

1. The hint: an L shaped tube with arms 5 and 5 has the same area as a straight tube of length 5 + 5 − 1 = 9, because the corner square is counted in both arms.
2. Add all the straight lengths: 20 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 5 = 120.
3. There are 8 bends, each counted twice, so subtract 8: 120 − 8 = 112.
4. The straightened tube is 112 units long and 1 unit wide: 112 × 1 = 112.
Answer: 112 square units

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 5): A square is divided into regions 1, 2 and 3. If the sidelength of the square is doubled, what is the increase in the areas of the regions 1, 2 and 3? Give reasons.
1. Doubling the side doubles every length in the figure, both across and up.
2. Each region's area is multiplied by 2 × 2 = 4.
3. So each region grows by 4 − 1 = 3 times its old area.
Answer: Each region becomes 4 times as big, an increase of 3 times its original area

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 6): Divide a square into 4 parts by drawing two perpendicular lines inside the square, then rearrange the pieces to get a larger square with a hole inside.
1. Draw two perpendicular lines through the square that are not parallel to its sides; the 4 pieces are congruent.
2. Turn the pieces so that each right angle points outward and the long edges run round the outside.
3. The outside forms a bigger square; the gap in the middle is a small square hole.
4. The area of the big square minus the hole equals the area of the original square.
Answer: The 4 congruent pieces form a larger square around a square hole; total area is unchanged

content.question: Identify the missing sidelengths. (i) A plus shaped figure is made of four rectangles: a 28 in² piece whose right edge rises 4 in above a 21 in² piece of length 7 in, a 35 in² piece of width 3 in plus the width of the 28 in² piece, and a 14 in² strip that hangs 2 in below the 35 in² piece; find the width of the 14 in² strip. content.q_figure: Figure (i): four rectangles joined in a pinwheel, with areas 28 in² at the top, 21 in² on the right, 35 in² on the left and 14 in² at the bottom, the lengths 3 in, 4 in, 7 in and 2 in marked and the width of the 14 in² rectangle shown as ? in; figure (ii): a rectangle 4 m tall made of a dotted 29 m² piece with a blank piece below it, an 11 m² hatched piece beside the top, the dotted piece and the blank piece together outlined and marked 50 m², and ? on the missing sides.

concepts.concept_name: Rectangles: Area Is Not Perimeter: Ans3

steps: (i) The 21 in² piece is 7 in long, so its height is 21 ÷ 7 = 3 in.
The 28 in² piece is 4 + 3 = 7 in tall, so its width is 28 ÷ 7 = 4 in.
The 35 in² piece is 3 + 4 = 7 in wide, so its height is 35 ÷ 7 = 5 in.
The 14 in² strip is 5 + 2 = 7 in tall, so its width is 14 ÷ 7 = 2 in.
(ii) Top widths: 29 ÷ 4 = 7.25 m and 11 ÷ 4 = 2.75 m.
The lower piece has area 50 − 29 = 21 m² and width 7.25 m, so its height is 21 ÷ 7.25 ≈ 2.9 m.
content.answer: (i) 2 in, with 3 in, 4 in and 5 in on the way. (ii) 7.25 m and 2.75 m across the top, and a lower height of 84/29 m, about 2.9 m

content.s_figure: Figure (i) with the unknown sides found as 3 in, 4 in, 5 in and 2 in, and figure (ii) with the top widths 7.25 m and 2.75 m and the lower height of about 2.9 m marked.

$1$. (i): The $21$ in$^2$ piece is $7$ in long, so its height is $21 \div 7 = 3$ in.
$2$. The $28$ in$^2$ piece is $4 + 3 = 7$ in tall, so its width is $28 \div 7 = 4$ in.

$5$. (ii): Top widths: $29 \div 4 = 7.25\text{ m}$ and $11 \div 4 = 2.75\text{ m}$.
$6$. The lower piece has area $50 - 29 = 21\text{ m}^2$ and width $7.25\text{ m}$, so its height is $21 \div 7.25 \approx 2.9\text{ m}$.
Answer: (i): $2$ in, with $3$ in, $4$ in and $5$ in on the way. (ii): $7.25\text{ m}$ and $2.75\text{ m}$ across the top, and a lower height of $\frac{84}{29}\text{ m}$, about $2.9\text{ m}$

tool_config.idea: Any side of a triangle can be the base. media.instructions_for_student: Any side of a triangle can be the base. Its height is the perpendicular distance from the opposite corner to the line of that base, which falls inside an acute triangle and outside an obtuse one, and 1/2 × base × height gives the same area for every choice. The slanting side is never the height.
media.description:
A triangle sits on a grid with a draggable dot at each corner. Tapping a side makes it the base and highlights it, and a dashed line drops from the opposite corner to the base with a small square marking the right angle. Readouts show the base, the height and half of base times height, and an Enclosing rectangle switch draws the rectangle with the same base and the same height round the triangle.

On every card the student first predicts which segment is the height, then taps to see it drawn. In the first card the base is 8 and the height is 5, and the student reads the area, 20 square units, noticing that it is half of the 8 by 5 rectangle that appears when the switch is on. The second card has base 5, slanting side 6 and height 4, and asks which number goes in the area. If the student uses the slanting side, the tool shows the larger wrong area, half of 5 times 6 which is 15, beside the true one, half of 5 times 4 which is 10. The third card is a right triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10. The student takes the side 10 as the base and finds that the height drawn to it is 4.8, and that half of 10 times 4.8 is 24, the same as half of 6 times 8.

Then the student drags the top corner sideways past the end of the base. The foot of the perpendicular slips off the base, so the tool extends the base line with a dotted line and keeps the height square to it, now outside the triangle. The fourth card asks for this with base 6 and height 4, and the area reads 12. In the fifth card a triangle with base 10 and height 6 has area 30; the student picks a second base, 12, the two products appear side by side, and the missing height comes out as 5. The sixth card asks the student to build a triangle of area 24 on a base of 8 by dragging the corner until the height reads 6.

Hints go in order. First: which side is the base, and which corner is opposite to it? Then: the height meets the base line at a right angle, so extend the base line if it has to. Then: take half of 8 times 5 and compare it with the area readout. Last, the area is written as 20 square units and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that any side can be the base, that the height is the perpendicular distance and never the slanting side, that it can fall outside the triangle, and that every choice of base gives the same area.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in two identical rectangles, X is near a corner and Y is in the middle of the top. Which triangle on DC is bigger?
2. Drop the altitude from X to DC. It cuts the rectangle into two smaller rectangles, and each is halved by a side of the triangle.
3. So the triangle is half of the left rectangle plus half of the right one: half the whole, wherever X is.

content.text:
To find the area of a triangle, what measurements do we need?
We need the sidelengths of the outer rectangle.
How do we get the outer rectangle from the given triangle?
BCDE is a rectangle (how?). Let us take its sidelengths to be height and base. Then, Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × base × height.
Since BXAE is a rectangle (how?), the height of the rectangle is the same as the height of the triangle.
Thus, if the height and the base of a triangle are known, we can find its area.
Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height.

content.text:
Worked example: A triangle has base 8 cm and height 5 cm. Find its area.
1. Its outer rectangle is 8 cm by 5 cm, area 8 × 5 = 40 cm².
2. The triangle is half of it.
3. Area = 1/2 × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².
Answer: 20 cm²

content.text:
Will this formula hold for the kind of triangle, around which we cannot draw a rectangle with BC as the base?
Here is one way to look at it. The area of ΔABC is the difference of the areas of ΔADC and ΔADB, each of which can be enclosed in a rectangle.
Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × h × DC − 1/2 × h × DB = 1/2 × h (DC − DB) = 1/2 × h × BC.
Thus, the area formula holds for all types of triangles.

content.text:
Worked example: In an obtuse triangle ABC the height from A meets CB extended at D, with h = 4 cm, DB = 3 cm and BC = 6 cm. Find the area.
1. DC = DB + BC = 3 + 6 = 9 cm.
2. Area of ΔADC = 1/2 × 4 × 9 = 18 cm². Area of ΔADB = 1/2 × 4 × 3 = 6 cm².
3. Area of ΔABC = 18 − 6 = 12 cm², and 1/2 × 4 × 6 = 12 cm² too.
Answer: 12 cm², the same as 1/2 × base × height

concepts.concept_name: When the height falls outside the triangle

content.text:
Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height.
The height is perpendicular to the chosen base, even when it falls outside the triangle.
A rectangle and a triangle have equal areas when the triangle has twice the rectangle's height on the same base, or twice its base with the same height.

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 3): Find the area of ΔSUB, given that it is isosceles, SE is perpendicular to UB, and the area of ΔSEB is 24 sq. units.
1. In an isosceles triangle the perpendicular from S to UB meets it at its midpoint, so UE = EB.
2. ΔSUE and ΔSEB have the same base length and the same height SE, so equal areas.
3. Area of ΔSUB = 24 + 24 = 48 sq. units.
Answer: 48 sq. units

ΔSUE and ΔSEB have the same base length and the same height SE, so equal areas.
Area of ΔSUB = 24 + 24 = 48 sq. units.

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 4): [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a rectangle into a triangle of equal area.
1. Take rectangle ABCD with base AB and height BC.
2. Extend AB to E so that BE = AB. Then AE is twice the base.
3. Join E to D. Triangle AED has base 2 × AB and height AD, so its area is 1/2 × 2AB × AD = AB × AD.
4. Another way: cut the rectangle along a diagonal and place the two halves side by side along the height to form one triangle.
Answer: A triangle on double the base with the same height (or double the height on the same base) has the rectangle's area

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 5): [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to transform a triangle into a rectangle of equal area.
1. Draw the height AX of triangle ABC on base BC.
2. Mark the midpoints of AB and AC and join them; this line is parallel to BC at half the height.
3. Drop perpendiculars from the two midpoints to BC. Cut off the two small top triangles and turn each into the gap below it.
4. The result is a rectangle with base BC and height 1/2 AX, so its area is 1/2 × BC × AX.
Answer: Cut along the line joining the midpoints of the two sides and swing the top pieces down: a rectangle on the same base with half the height

content.text:
$1$. Drop the altitude $XY$ to $DC$. It splits the rectangle into two rectangles.
$2$. Each small rectangle is cut in half by $XD$ or $XC$.
$3$. So $\triangle XDC$ is half of the whole rectangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 4 = 10\text{ cm}^2$.
Answer: $10\text{ cm}^2$

media.description:
The student sees a triangle ABC on a grid with BC along the bottom and a point D that slides along it. The line AD splits the triangle into a left part and a right part, shaded in two colours, and two bars beside the figure show the area of each part. A marker shows the midpoint of BC, and a Rectangle button switches the screen to a rectangle with both diagonals drawn and the four triangles shaded.

In the first card BC is 10 and the height is 6, and the student predicts where D must sit before touching it. Sliding D, the student watches one bar rise as the other falls. When D reaches the midpoint, 5 from B, the bars level out and turn green at 15 each. In the second card D is put 4 from B and the bars read 12 and 18. The third card asks for D so that the left part is a quarter of the triangle, which needs BD to be 2.5 and gives 7.5 out of 30. A wrong placement shows both areas written as half of a base times the same height, so the student sees that only the base differs. Where the two parts are equal in area but not alike in shape, the tool puts them side by side with their bases and the shared height, to correct the idea that equal areas need matching pieces.

In the fourth card the student switches to a rectangle 8 by 6 whose diagonals meet at O and reads the area of each of the four triangles, 12 each. The two thin triangles and the two fat ones are not congruent, but tapping any of them shows its base on half of a diagonal and the same altitude as its neighbour. In the fifth card D stays at the midpoint and the student slides the top corner along a line parallel to BC. The shapes of the two parts keep changing, yet the bars stay level, because the height does not change. In the sixth card BC is 12 and the height is 5, and the student finds BD so that the left part has area 10, which is 4.

Hints go in order. First: which two bases do the two parts stand on, and what height do they share? Then: equal heights mean the areas are equal exactly when the bases are equal. Then: with BC = 10 and height 6, the left part is half of BD times 6, so set it equal to 15. Last, D is shown at 5 from B, each part is half of 5 times 6, which is 15, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that a line from a corner to the midpoint of the opposite side halves the area, that equal areas do not need equal shapes, and that the same reasoning gives four equal-area triangles in a rectangle.

media.instructions_for_student: Triangles on the same base whose top vertex lies on a line parallel to the base all have the same height, so the same area. Their perimeters differ, and the smallest perimeter comes when the top vertex sits on the perpendicular bisector of the base, found by reflecting one end of the base in the line.
media.description:
Base BC is fixed near the bottom of a grid, and a straight line l runs parallel to it above. A draggable top vertex A sits on l, so the triangle ABC changes shape as A moves. Live readouts give the base, the height, the area and the perimeter, a height bar shows the distance from l to BC, and a Reflect button waits beside the figure.

In the first card the base is 6 and the height is 4. The student predicts whether the area will change as A slides, then drags A to three different places and records the area at each, 12 every time. If the student predicted a change, the height bar is highlighted as unchanged to show why. Meanwhile the perimeter readout keeps changing and leaves a trail of its values on the screen. The second card asks where on l the perimeter is the largest the student can find. Dragging A farther along l keeps raising the perimeter, so the student finds that there is no largest, only a lowest value, which the trail makes easy to see.

In the third card the student uses Reflect. The tool draws the mirror image C' of C in l, and the student draws the straight path from B to C'. A is placed where that path crosses l. The reflected path is drawn in a second colour and its length is shown. AC and AC' are equal, so the bent path B to A to C has the same length as B to A to C', and with A on the straight line this is the shortest it can be. The perimeter trail shows its lowest value here. The fourth card asks the student to check that AB equals AC at this point, which puts A on the perpendicular bisector of BC. In the fifth card the height is changed to 3 and the student predicts the new area, 9, before sliding. The sixth card gives AX = 3, BC = 5 and AC = 4. The student writes the area as half of 5 times 3, which is 7.5, writes it again with base AC as half of 4 times BY, and solves for BY, which is 3.75.

Hints go in order. First: which two measurements does the area of a triangle depend on? Then: is the distance from A to the base changing as A slides along l? Then: reflect C in l; the straight line from B to the image crosses l at the best A. Last, the best A is shown on the perpendicular bisector of BC and a new card follows. Through doing, the student learns that triangles on one base with the top vertex on a parallel line share one area but not one perimeter, that the smallest perimeter comes from reflection, and that one area written with two bases gives a missing altitude.

content.text:
Find BY.
BY can be found using the formula for the area of a triangle.
What is Area (ΔABC)?
Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × AX × BC = 15/2 sq. units.
The area of the triangle can also be written as Area (ΔABC) = 1/2 × BY × AC = 1/2 × 4 × BY = 2 BY.
Thus, 2 BY = 15/2. So, BY = 15/4 = 3.75 units.

content.text:
Are the 4 triangles obtained by drawing the diagonals of a rectangle (regions 1 to 4 in the figure) of equal areas?
Clearly, the triangles 1 to 4 are not four congruent triangles.
If OD and OB are taken as the bases, then we see that both triangles have the same altitude! We also have OB = OD, since the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other. So, the triangles 1 and 2 have equal areas.
In a triangle, the line joining a vertex to the midpoint of its opposite side divides the triangle into two triangles of equal areas.

content.text:
Worked example: The diagonals of an 8 cm by 6 cm rectangle meet at O. Find the area of each of the four triangles.
1. The rectangle has area 8 × 6 = 48 cm².
2. Adjacent triangles have equal halves of a diagonal as bases and the same height, so equal areas.
3. All four are equal: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm².
Answer: Each triangle is 12 cm², even though they are not congruent

1. Predict first: as the top vertex slides along l, does the area grow, shrink or stay the same?
2. Every triangle has base BC and the same height, the distance between the parallel lines.
3. So all the areas are equal: there is no largest or smallest. The perimeter does change: it keeps growing as the vertex slides far away, so there is no largest perimeter, but there is a smallest.

content.text:
Worked example: BC = 6 cm and line l is parallel to BC, 4 cm away. Find the area of a triangle on BC with its top on l, and say how it changes as the top moves.
1. Base = 6 cm, height = 4 cm for every position of the top.
2. Area = 1/2 × 6 × 4 = 12 cm².
3. Moving the top changes the slanting sides, not the height.
Answer: Always 12 cm²: equal areas; only the perimeter changes

content.text:
Intuition might suggest that the triangle with the minimum perimeter can be obtained by constructing the perpendicular bisector of BC. But how do we justify that this triangle has the least perimeter among all the triangles?
Let us imagine the line l as a mirror.
What can we say about the lengths of AB and its reflection AB′? Since ΔAXB ≅ ΔAXB′, AB = AB′.
So, finding point A that gives the shortest possible path B → A → C is the same as finding a point A that gives the shortest possible path B → A → C′. Choose A on the straight line BC′.
Analyse whether A lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is the top vertex for the shortest perimeter right above the middle of BC?
2. Reflect C in l to C′. Any path from A to C is as long as the path from A to C′.
3. The shortest way from B to C′ is a straight line. Where it crosses l is the best A, and by symmetry it is halfway along, on the perpendicular bisector of BC.

content.text:
Worked example: B and C are 3 cm below line l and BC = 8 cm. Find the smallest possible value of AB + AC with A on l.
1. Reflect C in l: C′ is 3 cm above l, so 6 cm above the line BC, directly over C.
2. BC′ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 6: √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10.
3. The straight line BC′ crosses l halfway across, above the midpoint of BC.
Answer: The smallest AB + AC is 10 cm, with A on the perpendicular bisector of BC

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 6): ABCD, BCEF and BFGH are identical squares, with H directly above B. The red region is the triangle DCH and the blue region is the part of square ABCD to the left of the line DH. (i) If the area of the red region is 49 sq. units, what is the area of the blue region? (ii) In another version, if the blue and red regions together are 180 sq. units, what is the area of each square?
1. Let each square have side s. Red: base DC = s, height CH = 2s, so area 1/2 × s × 2s, which is s².
2. DH rises 2s over a run of s, so it crosses AB at its midpoint: the blue triangle has legs s and s/2, area one quarter of s².
3. (i) s² = 49, so blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25 sq. units.
4. (ii) Blue + red is five quarters of s², so s² = 180 × 4 ÷ 5 = 144 sq. units.
Answer: (i) 12.25 sq. units (ii) 144 sq. units

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 7): If M and N are the midpoints of XY and XZ, what fraction of the area of ΔXYZ is the area of ΔXMN? (Hint: join NY.)
1. NY is a median of ΔXYZ (N is the midpoint of XZ), so ΔXNY is half of ΔXYZ.
2. In ΔXNY, NM is a median (M is the midpoint of XY), so ΔXMN is half of ΔXNY.
3. 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Answer: ΔXMN is 1/4 of ΔXYZ

content.text:
Figure it Out (triangles, question 8): Gopal needs to carry water from the river to his water tank. He starts from his house. What is the shortest path from his house to the river and then to the water tank? Recreate the map and trace it.
1. Treat the river bank as a mirror line and reflect the water tank to the far side of it.
2. Join the house to the reflected tank with a straight line.
3. Where this line meets the river bank is the best point to fill water.
4. Walk house to that point, then to the real tank: this is as long as the straight line, the shortest possible.
Answer: Reflect the tank in the river bank; the straight line from the house to the reflection meets the bank at the best point

content.question: In ΔABC, AX = 3 is the height to BC = 5, and AC = 4. Find the height BY to AC.
content.text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AX = 3$ is the height to $BC = 5$, and $AC = 4$. Find the height $BY$ to $AC$.
content.publication_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AX = 3$ is the height to $BC = 5$, and $AC = 4$. Find the height $BY$ to $AC$.
content.question_tex: In $\triangle ABC$, $AX = 3$ is the height to $BC = 5$, and $AC = 4$. Find the height $BY$ to $AC$.
content.q_figure: A triangle ABC with BC = 5 along the bottom, a perpendicular AX of length 3 from A to X on BC, the side AC = 4, and a perpendicular BY from B to the side AC meeting it at Y.

steps: Area = 1/2 × 3 × 5 = 7.5 square units.
Also, area = 1/2 × 4 × BY, which is 2 × BY.
So 2 × BY = 7.5, and BY = 7.5 ÷ 2 = 3.75 units.
content.answer: BY = 3.75 units
content.question: In ΔABC, AX = 3 is the height to BC = 5, and AC = 4. Find the height BY to AC.

content.book_number: Using the Area Formula: finding the height BY
content.text:
$1$. Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 5 = 7.5$ square units.
$2$. Also, area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times BY$, which is $2 \times BY$.
$3$. So $2 \times BY = 7.5$, and $BY = 7.5 \div 2 = 3.75\text{ units}$.
Answer: $BY = 3.75\text{ units}$

media.description: Three identical squares are placed in an L shape, with a red triangle and a blue triangle on them. The red triangle equals one whole square, the blue triangle is a quarter of a square, and these give the blue area and the area of each square.

video_script.why: The child applies the half of base times height method of the solved examples, reading the base and height off the sides of identical squares.

marks.sq: the three identical squares appear, two side by side and one on top of the right one
marks.ask: the red area 49 sq. units and a question mark on the blue region appear
marks.red: the triangle D C H fills red

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='sq'/>Two squares sit side by side, with a third square on top of the right one.
<bookmark mark='red'/>The red region is the triangle with corners D, C and H.
<bookmark mark='blue'/>The blue region is the part of the left square on the left of the line D H.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The red area is forty nine square units.
What is the area of the blue region?
<bookmark mark='two'/>In another picture, the blue and red regions together are one hundred eighty square units.
What is the area of each square?
beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; squares ABCD and BCEF side by side and square BFGH on top of BCEF; red triangle DCH; the part of ABCD left of line DH in blue; red area 49 sq. units

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Think and tell.

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Use the same method as before.
The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
<bookmark mark='rt'/>The base and the height meet at a right angle.
<bookmark mark='sides'/>Here, the equal sides of the squares give us both.
beats.on_screen: a triangle with its base and its height at a right angle; the rule area = 1/2 × base × height; the sides of the squares are equal

marks.areas: the two given areas are written
marks.given: the squares and the position of H are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three identical squares, with H straight above B.
<bookmark mark='areas'/>In the first picture, red is forty nine square units.
In the second, blue and red together are one hundred eighty.
beats.on_screen: Given: ABCD, BCEF, BFGH identical squares; H directly above B; (i) red = 49 sq. units; (ii) blue + red = 180 sq. units

marks.find: the two things to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the blue area in the first picture.
Then we find the area of each square in the second.
beats.on_screen: To find: (i) the blue area; (ii) the area of each square

marks.tri: the red triangle D C H is outlined with DC = s marked
marks.area: 1/2 × s × 2s = s² is written and the red triangle is shown as one whole square

narration: <bookmark mark='tri'/>Step one, take the red triangle D C H.
Its base D C is one side of a square.
<bookmark mark='ht'/>Its height C H is two sides, because C B and B H are both sides.
<bookmark mark='area'/>Half of one side times two sides is one whole square.
The red area equals one square, forty nine square units.
beats.on_screen: Red triangle DCH: base DC = s, height CH = 2s; area = 1/2 × s × 2s = s², one whole square = 49

marks.mid: the point where D H meets A B is marked at the middle of A B
marks.climb: the line D H is traced with its climb of two sides over one side across

narration: <bookmark mark='climb'/>Step two, look at the line D H.
It climbs two sides for every one side across.
<bookmark mark='mid'/>It climbs one side, the height of the left square, after half a side across.
It meets eigh B at its middle.
beats.on_screen: line DH climbs 2s for a run of s; after a run of s/2 it has climbed s, so it meets AB at its midpoint

marks.legs: the blue triangle shows one side going up and half a side across
marks.quarter: 1/2 × s × s/2 = s²/4 is written, one quarter of a square

narration: <bookmark mark='legs'/>Step three, the blue triangle has one side going up and half a side across.
<bookmark mark='quarter'/>Half of one side times half a side is a quarter of a square.
<bookmark mark='calc'/>Divide forty nine by four to get twelve point two five.
beats.on_screen: Blue triangle: legs s and s/2; area = 1/2 × s × s/2 = s²/4; blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25

marks.tog: blue + red = 1 square + 1/4 square is written

narration: <bookmark mark='tog'/>Step four, blue and red together make one square and a quarter of a square.
<bookmark mark='five'/>That is five quarters of a square, and it equals one hundred eighty.
<bookmark mark='calc'/>One quarter is one hundred eighty divided by five, which is thirty six.
<bookmark mark='whole'/>Four quarters make a whole square, so thirty six times four gives one hundred forty four.
<bookmark mark='chk'/>Check, one hundred forty four plus thirty six is one hundred eighty.
beats.on_screen: (ii) blue + red = 1 square + 1/4 square = 5/4 of a square = 180; 1/4 of a square = 180 ÷ 5 = 36; a square = 36 × 4 = 144; check: 144 + 36 = 180

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The blue region is twelve point two five square units.
Each square is one hundred forty four square units.
beats.on_screen: Answer: (i) 12.25 sq. units (ii) 144 sq. units

the line DH climbs 2s for a run of s, so it climbs s (the height of ABCD) after a run of s/2, and meets AB at its midpoint
blue triangle: legs s and s/2, area = 1/2 × s × s/2 = s²/4, one quarter of a square
(i) s² = 49, so blue = 49 ÷ 4 = 12.25 sq. units
(ii) blue + red = s² + s²/4 = 5s²/4 = 180, so s²/4 = 36 and s² = 144 sq. units (side 12)

media.description: In a triangle, M and N are the midpoints of two sides. A line from a corner to the midpoint of the opposite side halves a triangle, and doing this twice shows that the small triangle is a quarter of the big one.

video_script.why: The child applies the equal bases, same height method of the solved example twice, to halve the triangle and then halve it again.

<bookmark mark='tri'/>Here is a triangle X Y Z.
<bookmark mark='mid'/>M is the midpoint of X Y, and N is the midpoint of X Z.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What fraction of the area of triangle X Y Z is the area of triangle X M N?

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find what fraction of triangle X Y Z is triangle X M N.

narration: <bookmark mark='join'/>Step one, join N to Y.
It cuts the triangle into X N Y and N Y Z.
<bookmark mark='eq'/>The bases X N and N Z are equal, and both triangles have the same height from Y.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Their areas are equal, so triangle X N Y is half of triangle X Y Z.
beats.on_screen: Join NY. XN = NZ and the height from Y is the same, so area (XNY) = 1/2 × area (XYZ)

marks.eq: XM = MY is marked and the height from N to X Y is drawn for both parts
marks.tri: triangle X N Y is outlined and N M is drawn
marks.half: area (XMN) = 1/2 × area (XNY) is written

narration: <bookmark mark='tri'/>Step two, look at triangle X N Y.
The line N M goes to the middle of X Y.
<bookmark mark='eq'/>The bases X M and M Y are equal, and both parts share the height from N.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Triangle X M N is half of triangle X N Y.
beats.on_screen: In triangle XNY: XM = MY and the height from N is the same, so area (XMN) = 1/2 × area (XNY)

marks.chain: the two halves are chained: 1/2 of 1/2 of area (XYZ)

narration: <bookmark mark='chain'/>Step three, triangle X M N is half of a half of triangle X Y Z.
<bookmark mark='quarter'/>Half of a half is a quarter.
beats.on_screen: area (XMN) = 1/2 × 1/2 × area (XYZ) = 1/4 × area (XYZ)

marks.two: area (XMN) = 2 is written, and 2 is 1/4 of 8

narration: <bookmark mark='eight'/>Step four, check with an area of eight.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Half of eight is four.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Half of four is two, and two is a quarter of eight.
beats.on_screen: check: area (XYZ) = 8, area (XNY) = 4, area (XMN) = 2, and 2 is 1/4 of 8

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Triangle X M N is one quarter of triangle X Y Z.
beats.on_screen: Answer: ΔXMN is 1/4 of ΔXYZ

video_script.anchor: the book's triangle XYZ with M on XY and N on XZ, the midpoints of their sides, and the dotted line NY
video_script.design: One triangle all video. A line to a midpoint halves a triangle, and it is done twice. The check uses a made-up area of eight.
source: Figure it Out (triangles, question 7)
never_show: the answer before the answer beat
maths_rules: N is the midpoint of XZ, so XN = NZ; triangles XNY and NYZ have equal bases on XZ and the same height from Y, so they have equal areas
the two equal triangles fill ΔXYZ, so ΔXNY = 1/2 of ΔXYZ
M is the midpoint of XY, so XM = MY; triangles XMN and MYN have equal bases on XY and the same height from N, so they have equal areas
the two equal triangles fill ΔXNY, so ΔXMN = 1/2 of ΔXNY
ΔXMN = 1/2 × 1/2 of ΔXYZ = 1/4 of ΔXYZ
check: if ΔXYZ = 8, then ΔXNY = 4 and ΔXMN = 2, and 2 is 1/4 of 8

media.description: A water carrier walks from a house to a river bank and then to a water tank. The video treats the river bank as a mirror, reflects the tank, and joins the house to the reflection with a straight line. Where that line meets the bank is the best place to fill water.

<bookmark mark='map'/>A water carrier starts at a house.
<bookmark mark='walk'/>The carrier walks to the river to fill water, then walks on to the water tank.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the shortest path from the house to the river and then to the tank?

video_script.anchor: the book's map: a house, a river bank above it and a water tank, with the water carrier's walk from the house to the bank and on to the tank
video_script.design: One map all video. The river bank is a mirror, the tank is reflected, and the bent walk becomes a straight line. No numbers are given, so the answer is a method.

hold_back: Reflect the tank in the river bank; the straight line from the house to the reflection meets the bank at the best point
never_show: the answer before the answer beat
maths_rules: the river bank is a line l; the house H and the tank T are on the same side of it
reflect T in l to get T'; for every point P on l, PT = PT'
so HP + PT = HP + PT', which is the length of a path from H to T' that bends at P
the shortest path from H to T' is the straight line HT', so the best P is where HT' meets l
any other P on l gives a bent path H to P to T', which is longer than the straight line HT'
the walk is H to P to T, as long as the straight line HT'
video_script.payoff_line: The best spot is where the straight line meets the river bank

final_answer.value: Reflect the tank in the river bank; the straight line from the house to the reflection meets the bank at the best point

media.instructions_for_student: The area of a polygon on a grid comes from splitting it into triangles and rectangles whose areas add, or from enclosing it in a rectangle and taking the corner pieces away, and both routes give the same area.
media.description:
Before any line is drawn, the student meets a polygon on a grid with its corners on grid points and two route buttons beneath it, Split and Enclose. Choosing the route is the first decision on every card. With Split, the student taps two corners to draw a line, and each part is shaded and labelled with its area as soon as it is marked. With Enclose, the smallest rectangle round the figure appears, and the corner pieces left over can be lifted off one at a time, each carrying its own area.

The first card is a quadrilateral with a diagonal of 14 and heights of 4 on one side and 2 on the other. Splitting along the diagonal gives two triangles, half of 14 times 4 which is 28 and half of 14 times 2 which is 14, so the area is 42 square units. The second card is a house shaped pentagon, a 6 by 4 rectangle with a triangle of height 3 on its side of 6, so 24 plus 9 gives 33. The third card is a figure inside a 10 by 6 rectangle with two corner triangles removed, each with legs 4 and 3; the rectangle is 60 and the corners are 6 each, so the area is 48. The fourth card is an 8 by 5 rectangle with a 2 by 2 notch cut out of one edge, which is 40 minus 4, or 36. The fifth card is a quadrilateral with a diagonal of 12 and heights of 5 and 3, so 30 plus 18 gives 48.

A split that leaves a gap or an overlap shades the squares that are wrong, so the student can correct the lines. Each part carries its own area, so the final sum is built from visible pieces. In the sixth card the figure sits inside a 12 by 9 rectangle with two corner triangles removed, each with legs 6 and 3. The student must use both routes on it: Enclose gives 108 minus 18, which is 90, and Split into triangles and rectangles must give the same total. When the two routes agree, the matching totals are shown side by side and the student says in a sentence why they agree.

Hints go in order. First: which route would you try first, splitting or cutting out of a rectangle? Then: split into pieces whose areas you can find, or enclose the figure and take away the corners. Then: for the quadrilateral with diagonal 14, find the two triangle areas from the diagonal and its heights. Last, the two triangles are written out as 28 and 14, the area is 42 square units, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that the area of any polygon on a grid comes from triangles and rectangles, either added together or taken away from an enclosing rectangle, and that both routes give the same area.

content.text:
Area of any Polygon
How do we find the area of this quadrilateral? What measurements do we need for this?
If we join BD, the quadrilateral ABCD gets divided into two triangles. By finding their areas, we can find the area of ABCD.
Can any polygon be divided into triangles?
It can be seen that any polygon can be divided into triangles. Thus, by knowing how to compute the area of a triangle, we can find the area of any polygon.
One can derive special formulae to find the areas of a parallelogram, rhombus and trapezium.

content.text:
Worked example: A quadrilateral ABCD has diagonal BD = 10 cm. The heights from A and C to BD are 4 cm and 3 cm. Find its area.
1. Area of ΔABD = 1/2 × 10 × 4 = 20 cm².
2. Area of ΔBCD = 1/2 × 10 × 3 = 15 cm².
3. Area of ABCD = 20 + 15 = 35 cm².
Answer: 35 cm²

content.text:
Worked example: A pentagon is a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle with a triangle of height 3 cm on its 6 cm side. Find its area.
1. Rectangle: 6 × 4 = 24 cm².
2. Triangle: 1/2 × 6 × 3 = 9 cm².
3. Pentagon: 24 + 9 = 33 cm².
Answer: 33 cm²

content.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 2): Find the area of the shaded region FECD given that ABCD is a rectangle, with AB = 18 cm, BC = 10 cm, AE = 10 cm, EB = 8 cm, AF = 6 cm and FD = 4 cm.
1. Rectangle ABCD: 18 × 10 = 180 cm².
2. Unshaded ΔAEF: 1/2 × 10 × 6 = 30 cm². Unshaded ΔEBC: 1/2 × 8 × 10 = 40 cm².
3. Shaded region = 180 − 30 − 40 = 110 cm².
Answer: 110 cm²

content.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 3): What measurements would you need to find the area of a regular hexagon?
1. Join the centre to all six corners: six identical equilateral triangles.
2. Each triangle has a side of the hexagon as base and the distance from the centre to that side as height.
3. So the side length and the centre to side distance are enough: area = 6 × 1/2 × side × that distance.
Answer: The side length and the perpendicular distance from the centre to a side

content.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 4): What fraction of the total area of the rectangle is the area of the blue region? (Two blue triangles stand on the top and bottom sides of the rectangle, with their tips meeting at a point inside.)
1. Each blue triangle has a full side of the rectangle as base: the length L.
2. Their heights, from the shared point to the top and to the bottom, add up to the width W.
3. Blue = 1/2 × L × h1 + 1/2 × L × h2 = 1/2 × L × (h1 + h2) = 1/2 × L × W.
Answer: Half of the rectangle is blue

content.text:
Figure it Out (area of any polygon, question 5): Give a method to obtain a quadrilateral whose area is half that of a given quadrilateral.
1. Mark the midpoints of the four sides and join them in order.
2. Each corner triangle cut off is one quarter of the triangle made by a diagonal (both sides are halved).
3. The four corners together are one quarter of each pair of diagonal triangles, so half the quadrilateral; the inner quadrilateral is the other half.
Answer: Join the midpoints of the sides in order; the inner quadrilateral has half the area

content.question: Find the area of the quadrilateral ABCD given that AC = 22 cm, BM = 3 cm, DN = 3 cm, BM is perpendicular to AC, and DN is perpendicular to AC.
content.s_figure: The same quadrilateral split by AC into the triangles ABC and ACD, each marked with base 22 cm, height 3 cm and area 33 cm².
content.text:
$1$. The diagonal $AC$ splits $ABCD$ into $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ACD$.
$2$. Area of $\triangle ABC = \frac{1}{2} \times 22 \times 3 = 33\text{ cm}^2$. Area of $\triangle ACD = \frac{1}{2} \times 22 \times 3 = 33\text{ cm}^2$.
$3$. Area of $ABCD = 33 + 33 = 66\text{ cm}^2$.
Answer: $66\text{ cm}^2$

media.instructions_for_student: Cutting a right triangle off one end of a parallelogram along a height and sliding it to the other end makes a rectangle with the same base and height, so the area of a parallelogram is base times height, using any side as base with its own perpendicular height.
media.description:
A parallelogram rests on a grid with its lower side marked as the base. A dashed cut line can be dragged along the base and always stays square to it, and a right angle marker shows where it meets the base. Readouts give the base, the height, the slanting side and the area, and a Change base button turns the figure so another side becomes the base.

In the first card the base is 7 and the height is 4. The student predicts whether a rectangle made from the same pieces will have the same area, then drags the cut line to the top corner. A right triangle comes away from the end. The student drags this triangle to the other end of the parallelogram, and when it fits exactly, the rectangle outline lights up with its area, 28. If the student tries to tilt the cut away from the right angle, the cut is refused and the right angle marker is shown. If the student reads the area from the slanting side instead of the height, the two areas are shown disagreeing, with the slanting side giving too much. The second card has base 5 and height 3, and the student reads the area, 15, and answers whether the slanting side was used anywhere. It was not.

In the third card the student builds three different parallelograms on the same base and height by sliding the top side along, and compares them. The slant changes, but the rectangle made by cut and slide is always the same, so the areas match. The fourth card puts a rectangle and a parallelogram, both with sides 5 and 4, side by side on the same base. The rectangle covers 20 squares, and the parallelogram, whose height is less than 4, covers fewer.

In the fifth card the sides are 12 and 7.6 and the height on the side of 12 is 6, so the area is 72. The student uses it to find the height on the other side, 72 divided by 7.6, which is about 9.47. In the sixth card the student presses Change base, uses the other side as the base, cuts again with its own height, and gets the same area.

Hints go in order. First: what shape do you get if the slanting ends become upright? Then: cut along a height so the piece is a right triangle. Then: the rectangle has the same base and the same height, so multiply them. Last, the cut and slide is shown with the area and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that a parallelogram can be turned into a rectangle of equal area by cutting off a right triangle and sliding it across, that area is base times height for either side taken as the base, and that the slanting side is never the height.

content.text:
Parallelogram
Give a method to convert a parallelogram into a rectangle of equal area.
Construct AX perpendicular to CD. We call this a height of the parallelogram. Cut the parallelogram into ΔAXD and trapezium ABCX.
Can ΔAXD and ABCX fit together, as shown in the figure, to get a rectangle?
So, by the RHS congruency criterion, ΔBYC ≅ ΔAXD. Thus, ΔAXD will fit exactly over the region occupied by ΔBYC, and convert the parallelogram into a rectangle.
The process of cutting a figure into pieces and rearranging them to get a different figure of equal area is called dissection.

1. Predict first: if we cut a parallelogram and move a piece, can it become a rectangle of the same area?
2. Cut along the height from one top corner. A right triangle comes away.
3. Slide it to the other end: it matches the gap exactly, because the two right triangles are congruent. Nothing is added or lost. This cut and rearrange is called dissection.

How do we find the area of a parallelogram by dissecting it into a rectangle?
Since DX = CY, we get DC = XY by adding the common part XC to DX and CY. Since DC is the base of the parallelogram, we get
Area of the parallelogram = base × height.
Can the area of the parallelogram be determined by taking another side as the base and its corresponding height?
Can the parallelogram be cut along CZ and rearranged to form a rectangle?
It can be seen that this is indeed possible, and so any side and its corresponding height can be used to find the area of a parallelogram.

Worked example: A parallelogram has sides 10 cm and 6 cm. The height on the 10 cm side is 4.8 cm. Find the area and the height on the 6 cm side.
1. Area = 10 × 4.8 = 48 cm².
2. With base 6 cm: 6 × height = 48.
3. Height = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm.
Answer: Area 48 cm²; the height on the 6 cm side is 8 cm

Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 4): Consider a rectangle and a parallelogram of the same sidelengths: 5 cm and 4 cm. Which has the greater area? (Hint: imagine constructing them on the same base.)
1. Rectangle: 5 × 4 = 20 cm².
2. On the same 5 cm base, the parallelogram's height is shorter than its slanting 4 cm side.
3. So its area, 5 × height, is less than 20 cm².
Answer: The rectangle has the greater area

Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 5): Give a method to obtain a rectangle whose area is twice that of a given triangle. What are the different methods that you can think of?
1. Method 1: draw a line through the top vertex parallel to the base and perpendiculars to the base at its ends; the rectangle on the base and height is twice the triangle.
2. Method 2: take two copies of the triangle, join them into a parallelogram, then cut and slide it into a rectangle.
3. Either way the rectangle is base × height, twice 1/2 × base × height.
Answer: Build the rectangle on the base and height, or join two copies into a parallelogram and cut and slide

Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 6): [Śulba-Sūtras] Give a method to obtain a rectangle of the same area as a given triangle.
1. Join the midpoints of the two sides; this line is parallel to the base at half the height.
2. Drop perpendiculars from these midpoints to the base.
3. Cut off the two small top pieces and turn each down into the gap below it.
4. The result is a rectangle with the same base and half the height: 1/2 × base × height.
Answer: Cut at half the height and swing the top pieces down: a rectangle on the base with half the height

Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 7): [Śulba-Sūtras] An isosceles triangle can be converted into a rectangle by dissection in a simpler way. Can you find out how to do it? (Hint: show that ΔADB and ΔADC can be made into halves of a rectangle.)
1. The altitude AD of isosceles ΔABC meets BC at its midpoint, giving two congruent right triangles.
2. Turn ΔADC over and place it against ΔADB with the hypotenuses together.
3. The two right triangles form a rectangle with sides BD and AD, area 1/2 × BC × AD.
Answer: Cut along the altitude and join the two right triangles along their slanting sides to make a rectangle BD by AD

Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 9): Which has greater area: an equilateral triangle or a square of the same sidelength as the triangle? Which has greater area: two identical equilateral triangles together or a square of the same sidelength as the triangle? Give reasons.
1. Square of side s: area s × s.
2. The triangle's height is less than its slanting side s, so its area is less than 1/2 × s × s.
3. Two triangles make a rhombus with base s and height less than s, so less than s × s too.
Answer: The square is greater in both cases

The triangle's height is less than its slanting side s, so its area is less than 1/2 × s × s.
Two triangles make a rhombus with base s and height less than s, so less than s × s too.

content.question: Which has greater area: an equilateral triangle or a square of the same sidelength as the triangle? Which has greater area: two identical equilateral triangles together or a square of the same sidelength as the triangle? Give reasons.
content.publication_text:
Figure it Out (parallelograms, question 9): Which has greater area: an equilateral triangle or a square of the same sidelength as the triangle? Which has greater area: two identical equilateral triangles together or a square of the same sidelength as the triangle? Give reasons.
1. Square of side s: area s × s.
2. The triangle's height is less than its slanting side s, so its area is less than 1/2 × s × s.
3. Two triangles make a rhombus with base s and height less than s, so less than s × s too.
Answer: The square is greater in both cases

media.instructions_for_student: Cutting a rhombus along both diagonals gives four right triangles that rearrange into a rectangle as long as one diagonal and as wide as half the other, so the area is 1/2 × d1 × d2. The full product of the diagonals is the rectangle drawn round the rhombus, which has twice the area.
media.description:
A rhombus is drawn in the middle of the screen with its two diagonals as dashed lines crossing at right angles. Each diagonal has a handle at one end. Dragging a handle lengthens or shortens that diagonal while the two diagonals keep crossing at their midpoints, so the rhombus changes shape but stays a rhombus. Readouts show d1, d2, the side and the area. Below the figure are a Cut button, an empty rectangle outline, and a switch that draws the rectangle round the rhombus.

In the first card the diagonals are 12 and 8. The student predicts what the pieces will make, then presses Cut. The rhombus separates into four right triangles with legs 6 and 4. The student drags them into the outline. Pieces that do not fit leave a gap, and the gap is shaded. When all four fit, the rectangle lights up with its two sides marked, 12 for a whole diagonal and 4 for half of the other, and the area reads 12 times 4, which is 48. Then the student switches on the rectangle round the rhombus, 12 by 8, and sees that it is twice as large, 96. This is why the full product of the diagonals is not the area; half of it is.

The second card has diagonals 10 and 6, and the student finds the area, 30. The third has diagonals 16 and 30; the rectangle is 30 by 8, or 16 by 15, and the area is 240. In the fourth card one diagonal is 12 and the area is 60, and the student drags the other handle until the area reads 60, which makes the other diagonal 10 and the rectangle 12 by 5. The fifth card has diagonals 6 and 8. The student finds the area, 24, and also the side, because each small triangle has legs 3 and 4, so the side is 5. In the sixth card the student makes a different rhombus with area 48, for example diagonals 16 and 6, and checks that the product of the diagonals is 96.

Hints go in order. First: what shapes do the two diagonals cut the rhombus into? Then: fit the four triangles into a rectangle; one side is a whole diagonal, the other is half of the other diagonal. Then: for diagonals 12 and 8 the rectangle is 12 by 4, so multiply those two sides. Last, the area is written as 12 times 4, which is 48 square units and is half of 12 times 8, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that the diagonals of a rhombus cut it into four triangles that rearrange into a rectangle, so the area is half of one diagonal times the other, never the whole product.

content.text:
Rhombus
Since a rhombus is a parallelogram, the area formula for a parallelogram holds for a rhombus as well. However, the additional properties of a rhombus give us another method to transform a rhombus into a rectangle of the same area by dissection. This method occurs in one of the Śulba-Sūtras.
Try working this out!
What are the sidelengths of the rectangle WXYZ?
XW = length of the diagonal AC, and WZ = half the length of the other diagonal BD.
Area of a rhombus = 1/2 × product of diagonals.

2. The diagonals cross at right angles and halve each other, so they cut four right triangles.
3. Pair them into two small rectangles and stack them: one whole diagonal by half the other.

content.text:
Worked example: A rhombus has diagonals 12 cm and 8 cm. Dissect it into a rectangle and find the area.
1. The rectangle has one side 12 cm, the whole diagonal.
2. Its other side is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm, half the other.
3. Area = 12 × 4 = 48 cm².
Answer: 48 cm²

Worked example: A rhombus has diagonals 10 cm and 6 cm. Find its area using two triangles.
1. Each triangle has base 10 cm and height 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.
2. Each triangle: 1/2 × 10 × 3 = 15 cm².
3. Rhombus: 15 + 15 = 30 cm², and 1/2 × 10 × 6 = 30 cm².
Answer: 30 cm²

content.text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 2): Give a method to convert a rectangle into a rhombus of equal area using dissection.
1. Cut the rectangle (length L, width W) into two halves, each L/2 long and W wide.
2. Cut each half along a diagonal: four congruent right triangles with legs L/2 and W.
3. Arrange them with the right angles meeting at one centre point: a rhombus with diagonals L and 2W.
4. Its area is 1/2 × L × 2W = L × W, the rectangle's area.
Answer: Cut into four congruent right triangles and put the right angles together at the centre

media.instructions_for_student: Two copies of a trapezium, one turned half way round and joined along a slanting side, make a parallelogram whose base is the sum of the parallel sides and whose height is the trapezium's height, so the trapezium is half of it: one half times height times the sum of the parallel sides.
media.description:
A single trapezium stands on the work surface with its parallel sides marked a and b, its height h shown as a dashed perpendicular, and editable boxes for a, b and h. A Copy button sits beside it, and once a copy exists it carries a rotate handle. Readouts show the base, the height and the area of whatever figure the two trapeziums make.

The student first predicts what shape two copies will make when joined. Pressing Copy places a second trapezium. The student turns it half way round with the handle and drags it to a slanting side, and when the slanting sides meet, the copy snaps into place. The angles at the joint add to 180 degrees, so the edges run straight, with the short side of one continuing the long side of the other, and the long base is labelled a + b. A copy joined without turning leaves a six sided figure, and the tool hints to rotate it. The student reads the base of the new parallelogram, compares it with a plus b, and halves its area to get the trapezium. A result that forgets the half is shown next to the parallelogram's area.

In the first card the parallel sides are 7 and 11 and the height is 6, so the parallelogram has base 18 and area 108, and the trapezium has area 54. In the second card the sides are 24 and 36 and the height is 14; the student predicts the parallelogram base, 60, first, then finds 840 for the parallelogram and 420 for the trapezium. In the third card the student changes only the height and watches the area change in step with it. The fourth card asks for a trapezium with area 144, so a plus b times h must be 288, for example sides 10 and 14 with height 12. In the fifth card the trapezium has both slants leaning the same way, and the student joins two copies and finds that the result is still a parallelogram with base a + b and height h. In the sixth card the student breaks the 7 and 11 trapezium instead into a rectangle and two triangles by dropping two heights, 7 times 6 is 42 plus two triangles of 12 in all, and compares the 54 with the first method.

Hints go in order. First: what shape has opposite sides parallel and an easy area? Then: turn the copy so its long side lines up with the short side of the first. Then: the base becomes a + b and the height stays h, so the parallelogram is a + b times h. Last, the joined parallelogram and its half are shown and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that two copies of any trapezium make a parallelogram, so the area of a trapezium is half of its height times the sum of the parallel sides.

Consider a trapezium WXYZ with WX ∥ ZY. Find its area.
Construct WM ⊥ ZY, and XN ⊥ ZY (WM and XN perpendicular to ZY).
Is WXNM a rectangle?
Area WXYZ = Area (ΔWMZ) + Area WXNM + Area (ΔXNY).
Can the area of the trapezium be expressed in terms of a, b and h?
Area of a trapezium = 1/2 × height × sum of the parallel sides.

Worked example: A slanting trapezium has parallel sides AB = 6 cm and DC = 10 cm and height 5 cm. Use Approach 2 to find its area.
1. Parallelogram ABGD: 6 × 5 = 30 cm².
2. Triangle BGC has base 10 − 6 = 4 cm: 1/2 × 4 × 5 = 10 cm².
3. Total = 30 + 10 = 40 cm², and 1/2 × 5 × (6 + 10) = 40 cm².
Answer: 40 cm²

content.text:
Finding the Area Using Two Copies of the Trapezium
Consider two copies of the given trapezium in which AB ∥ CD. Rotate the second copy as shown.
What figure will we get when the two trapeziums are joined along BC?
Since AB ∥ CD, we have x + y = 180, since they are internal angles along the same side of the transversal (BC). Therefore, the resulting figure is a quadrilateral.
What type of a quadrilateral is this?
Area of the trapezium = 1/2 × Area of the parallelogram = 1/2 h(a + b).

1. Predict first: two copies of a trapezium, one turned round, joined along a slanting side. What shape?
2. The angles at the joint add to 180, so the edges run straight: the short side of one continues the long side of the other, making a side a + b long.
3. Opposite sides are parallel: a parallelogram of area (a + b) × h, and the trapezium is half of it.

Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 5): Here is one of the ways to convert trapezium ABCD into a rectangle EFGH of equal area. Given the trapezium ABCD, how do we find the vertices of the rectangle EFGH? (Hint: if ΔAHI ≅ ΔDGI and ΔBEJ ≅ ΔCFJ, then the trapezium and rectangle have equal areas.)
1. Mark I and J, the midpoints of the slanting sides AD and BC.
2. Through I draw the line perpendicular to DC; it meets DC at G and the line AB extended at H.
3. Through J do the same to get F on DC and E on AB extended.
4. Since AI = DI and the angles match, ΔAHI ≅ ΔDGI and ΔBEJ ≅ ΔCFJ, so EFGH has the trapezium's area.
Answer: Take the midpoints I and J of the slanting sides and draw perpendiculars to DC through them; they meet DC and line AB at G, H, F and E

Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 6): Using the idea of converting a trapezium into a rectangle of equal area, and vice versa, construct a trapezium of area 144 cm².
1. A trapezium has the area of a rectangle with sides h and 1/2 × (a + b).
2. Choose a 12 cm by 12 cm rectangle: area 144 cm². So h = 12 and a + b = 24.
3. Take a = 8 and b = 16: 1/2 × 12 × (8 + 16) = 144.
Answer: For example, parallel sides 8 cm and 16 cm with height 12 cm (any a + b and h with h × (a + b) = 288 works)

3. The rhombus is 2 of them and the equilateral triangle is 1.
Answer: Trapezium : triangle : rhombus = 3 : 1 : 2

content.text:
Figure it Out (rhombus and trapezium, question 8): ZYXW is a trapezium with ZY ∥ WX. A is the midpoint of XY. Show that the area of the trapezium ZYXW is equal to the area of ΔZWB, where ZA extended meets WX extended at B.
1. YA = XA, since A is the midpoint of XY.
2. ∠ZAY = ∠BAX (vertically opposite) and ∠ZYA = ∠BXA (alternate angles, since ZY ∥ WB).
3. So ΔZYA ≅ ΔBXA (ASA): they have equal areas.
4. Trapezium ZYXW = ZAXW + ΔZYA = ZAXW + ΔBXA = ΔZWB.
Answer: ΔZYA ≅ ΔBXA, so swapping one for the other shows the trapezium and ΔZWB have equal areas

video_script.anchor: an isosceles trapezium with its top side, bottom side and height marked
video_script.design: One isosceles trapezium stays all video. The midpoint lines cut a small triangle off each bottom corner, and each triangle turns half way round about its midpoint into the gap above it, so the pieces make a rectangle.
source: Convert an isosceles trapezium to a rectangle by cutting it into pieces, from the Sulba Sutras
maths_rules: isosceles trapezium: slanting sides equal, top side a, bottom side b, height h
mark the midpoint of each slanting side
through each midpoint draw the line at right angles to the parallel sides
each line cuts off a small corner triangle below the midpoint; it is congruent to the gap triangle above the midpoint (equal angles at the midpoint, right angles, equal halves of the slanting side)
turn each corner triangle half way round about its midpoint into the gap above it
the result is a rectangle of height h and length 1/2 x (a + b), with the same area as the trapezium
video_script.payoff_line: It becomes a rectangle. Its height is the same, and its length is half the sum of the parallel sides.

final_answer.value: rectangle of height h and length 1/2 × (a + b)
final_answer.spoken: a rectangle as tall as the trapezium and as long as half the sum of the parallel sides

video_script.substitution: The book question gives no numbers, so the sides are called the top side, the bottom side and the height.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: cut at the midpoints of the slanting sides and turn each corner piece about its midpoint. Watch for students who cut anywhere along the slanting side, because then the pieces do not fit.

media.description: A trapezium ABCD is turned into a rectangle EFGH of the same area. maths_rules: trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to DC
I is the midpoint of AD and J is the midpoint of BC
the line through I at right angles to DC meets DC at G and the line AB extended at H
the line through J at right angles to DC meets DC at F and the line AB extended at E

media.title: How do we draw a trapezium with a chosen area?
media.context: Area. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A trapezium has the same area as a rectangle as tall as the trapezium and as long as half the sum of its parallel sides. So we choose a rectangle of area one hundred forty four square centimetres, read off the height and the sum of the parallel sides, and pick two sides that add up to it.

video_script.why: The child knows the rule for the area of a trapezium and now works backwards from a chosen rectangle to the sides of a trapezium.

maths_rules: area of a trapezium = 1/2 x h x (a + b) = h x (1/2 x (a + b)), the area of a rectangle with sides h and 1/2 x (a + b)

choose a = 8, then b = 24 - 8 = 16

modules.module_summary: Real objects are measured in square centimetres, square inches, square feet, acres and square kilometres. Students convert between units, estimate the areas of tables, rooms, schools and towns, and close with a summary.

segments.summary: Real areas use many units: cm², in², ft², m², acres and km². A square unit converts by the length factor squared, so 1 in² = 6.4516 cm² and 1 km² = 1000000 m².

tool_config.idea: When one unit is k times as long as another, a square of the larger unit holds k × k squares of the smaller, so a square unit converts by the length factor multiplied by itself: 1 square foot is 12 × 12 = 144 square inches, and 1 square inch is 2.54 × 2.54 = 6.4516 square centimetres (a factor that is not whole leaves partial squares and strips in the tiling).

media.instructions_for_student: When one unit is k times as long as another, a square of the larger unit holds k × k squares of the smaller, so a square unit converts by the length factor multiplied by itself: 1 square foot is 12 × 12 = 144 square inches, and 1 square inch is 2.54 × 2.54 = 6.4516 square centimetres (a factor that is not whole leaves partial squares and strips in the tiling).
media.description:
One large unit square fills the middle of the screen, with a pair chooser above it offering metre and centimetre, foot and inch, inch and centimetre, and kilometre and metre. Two readouts show the length factor and the area factor, and a converter row below turns a given area from one unit into the other.

Each card begins with a prediction typed into the area factor box before the square is tiled. Then the student chooses a pair, and the side of the big square splits into equal parts. For foot and inch it splits into 12 parts along each side, and the whole square fills with small squares in 12 rows of 12. The tool counts by rows, so the area factor appears as rows times columns, 12 times 12, which is 144. A student who types the length factor 12 as the area factor sees a tiling in which 12 squares cover only one row, so it visibly does not fit. Metre and centimetre give 100 times 100, which is 10000. For kilometre and metre the tool shows a zoomed corner of the tiling with the count written beside it, 1000 rows of 1000, which is 1000000 square metres.

The inch and centimetre pair is the surprise, because 2.54 is not a whole number. The tiling shows 2 by 2 whole centimetre squares, two thin strips each 2 by 0.54, and a tiny corner piece 0.54 by 0.54. These add up to 4 plus 2.16 plus 0.2916, which is 6.4516 square centimetres, so the student sees why 1 square inch is not 2.54 square centimetres. The first four cards ask for 1 square foot in square inches (144), 1 square metre in square centimetres (10000), 1 square inch in square centimetres with the reason it is not 2.54 (6.4516), and 1 square kilometre in square metres (1000000). Then the converter row is used. The fifth card turns 12.9032 square centimetres into square inches by dividing by 6.4516, which gives 2. The sixth card turns a room of 20 square metres into square centimetres by multiplying by 10000, which gives 200000. A correct conversion shows the factor used and the converted area.

Hints go in order. First: how many small squares fit along one side, and how many rows are there? Then: the area factor is the length factor times itself, because the squares fill rows and columns. Then: for feet and inches the length factor is 12, so multiply 12 by 12. Last, 1 square foot is shown as 12 times 12, which is 144 square inches, and a similar card follows. Through doing, the student learns that a square unit converts by the length factor multiplied by itself, and can explain why the area factor is the length factor used twice.

media.description: One inch is two point five four centimetres, so inches are changed to centimetres by multiplying and centimetres to inches by dividing. content.text:
Worked example: A classroom is 8 m by 6 m. How many such classrooms would fit in 1 km²?
1. Classroom: 8 × 6 = 48 m².
2. 1 km² = 1000 × 1000 = 1000000 m².
3. 1000000 ÷ 48 ≈ 20833 classrooms.
Answer: About 20833 classrooms

content.text:
In-text question (areas in real life, question 3): How many times is your village/town/city bigger than your school?
1. Write both areas in the same unit, for example m².
2. For a school ground 100 m by 80 m: 100 × 80 = 8000 m². For a town of 10 km²: 10 × 1000000 = 10000000 m².
3. Divide: 10000000 ÷ 8000 = 1250.
Answer: For a 10 km² town and an 8000 m² school, 1250 times; use your own town and school data

topics.summary: Triangle, polygon, parallelogram, rhombus and trapezium areas, each found by cutting and rearranging into rectangles and triangles.

content.text:
Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height.
The area of any polygon can be evaluated by breaking it into triangles.
Area of a parallelogram = base × height.
Area of a rhombus = 1/2 × product of its diagonals.
Area of a trapezium = 1/2 × height × sum of parallel sides.

content.text:
1. Our opening puzzle is settled: a square can be cut into four equal areas in endless ways, because area counts squares, not shapes.
2. A triangle is half a rectangle; any polygon is a set of triangles; a parallelogram slides into a rectangle; a rhombus is half the rectangle on its diagonals; two trapeziums make a parallelogram.
3. Every height is perpendicular to its base. Still open for you: estimate the area of your town.
